item.title: Jensen Huang Returns, TrumpCare, Woke Socialism
item.description:
Robby Soave and Christian Britschgi kick off this episode of Freed Up by sharing their mixed feelings about Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO. Next, they react to Robert Pattinson's selection as the new James Bond, and Christian pans the 2021 film No Sudden Move . Turning back to politics, the boys discuss Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's (D–Mich.) proposal for TrumpCare and Meagan Day's New York Times article on Woke 1.0. The episode wraps up with an extended discussion of the Democrats' 2027 debate schedule and the (limited) usefulness of our primary system. If you enjoy Freed Up , be sure to watch our live episode Thursday, December 3 at 12 p.m. Eastern: https://www.youtube.com/live/iE81g2jyAoU 0:00—Huang is reinstated as Nvidia CEO. 6:40—It's all political. 14:14—Certain tech CEOs are irreplaceable. 17:30—Pattinson is the new Bond. 21:10— No Sudden Move (2021) is a terrible film.…

item.title: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city
item.description:
Abelardo de la Espriella to take control of an operation involving scores of security personnel trying to free at least 20 hostages Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city. Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of a operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces. item.description:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed runners-up.

item.title: Meta and other social media firms are not liable for Buffalo mass shooting, court rules
item.description:
The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation won a crucial victory against the Trump administration in court on Tuesday in a case challenging the president’s right to sell early access to his social media posts on Truth Social. The ruling by Judge J. Paul Oetken in the Southern District of New York allows both organizations to seek limited discovery, offering a chance to peel back the layers on the president’s scheme to enrich himself through his public office. The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation can request records from the president’s private media company on both the operation of its six-figure early-access model and whether other media companies have purchased a subscription. Truth Social is owned and operated by Trump Media & Technology Group, a company in which the president holds the largest stake in a trust controlled by his son, Donald Trump Jr. The…

Sources: Reason, The Guardian, The Intercept

item.title: States sue HUD over a rule that would end housing aid for mixed-status families
item.description:
A Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that could force thousands of mixed-immigration-status families to either move out of their homes or separate has been hit with further legal challenges: one filed by a group of cities facing affordable housing shortages, including San Francisco and New York, and the other by twenty states and Washington, DC. The rule, set to take effect December 14, would deny housing assistance to any tenants who live with people who don’t verify their immigration status, potentially affecting more than 20,000 households that currently receive federal support. The lawsuits argue that the HUD rule violates a provision in the Housing and and Community Development Act that Congress established to prevent family separations. And the cities suing, which include among others New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, and Boston, say the rule will…

Covered by 3 nonprofit.
Sources: CalMatters, Mother Jones, PBS NewsHour

item.title: Colombian president blames ex-FARC rebels for car bomb blast
item.description:
A car bomb detonated in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio on Monday, destroying a local governor's office and surrounding buildings, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. The right-wing leader has conducted a major crackdown on the country's drug trade, in response to left-wing FARC rebels who have stepped up attacks over the past two years. FRANCE 24's Daniel Whittington reports.

Covered by 3 public.
Sources: Al Jazeera English, BBC News, France 24

item.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
item.description:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Eleven days. One Scaramucci. There’s milk in my refrigerator that was bought before Jensen Huang’s downfall, and I may pour a glass to mark his return. To review: Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 after revelations that he’d had an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy who’d routed embargoed Nvidia chips to Chinese AI companies. Huang allegedly also had an affair with an executive who was one of his 60 direct reports at Nvidia. Five days after the resignation, Nvidia’s board chair, Harvey Jones, said the company “ does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO .” Five days after that, President Trump posted that he hoped it would. This morning, citing “input from senior levels of the United States government,” the board voted unanimously to let him come back. So…

item.title: Live: Two Libyan soldiers killed in Ukrainian attack on Russian vessels in Benghazi
item.description:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government. item.title: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
item.description:
Charli James is pleased to welcome Gavin Hall, Teaching Fellow in Political Science, and International Security at the University of Strathclyde. Hall examines recent Russian and Ukrainian operations beyond the main conflict zone, the conditions necessary for a negotiated settlement and the implications of diminishing direct US military support for Ukraine. “Both sides are prepared to operate beyond the main battleground and outside of the conflict zone,” he explains. Hall discusses why both sides want to negotiate from a position of strength and the conditions under which a “mutually hurting stalemate” could lead to a negotiated settlement.

Covered by 2 public.
Sources: BBC News, France 24
